name: Village Enterprise: poverty graduation in East Africa (charityevals)
summary: Village Enterprise runs a one-year poverty graduation program for the poorest rural households in Uganda, Kenya, Rwanda, Ethiopia and Tanzania: business training, seed grants to groups of three entrepreneurs, mentoring and savings groups, a third of it (DREAMS) in refugee settlements with Mercy Corps in Uganda and Ethiopia and through local organisations in Tanzania. Against its fiscal year 2025 spending (US$21.0M with overhead, 47,505 households), two randomized trials of the program itself (consumption 7.3% higher in Kenya, 3.6% in Uganda, 17% in DREAMS and 13% for its refugees, among all households offered the program) give about 4 years of healthy life per $1,000, close to GiveDirectly. The biggest uncertainty is how long the consumption gain lasts: the trials followed households for at most 2.5 years after the program, and the model assumes a gain fading 5% a year for 8 years (3 to 12).

Every program is a version of the same one-year poverty graduation model (training, seed grants to business groups of three, mentoring, savings groups), so all of it is counted against all the entrepreneurs it trained. That includes the refugee program DREAMS (32% of program spending, its own branch below), the nutrition-adapted program in northern Kenya (Nawiri, 6%, ended early in 2025) and the work helping the Kenyan and Rwandan governments adopt the model (no spending split, no outcome count; its benefit beyond the people Village Enterprise trained is in unmodelled_benefits_adj).

rows.label: Yearly increase in ln(consumption), DREAMS Ethiopia (refugee camps)
rows.explainer: Ethiopia's DREAMS households are all refugees, in three camps in Dollo Ado, so they take the trial's refugee effect on participants (about 14%), not the all-household one. Its further doubt (Somali camps rather than South Sudanese settlements in Uganda) is in dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS in Ethiopia's camps (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Internal validity of the trial (0.95, as core_evidence_adj) times its carry to Ethiopia (0.85). The Uganda trial's refugee effect carried to Ethiopia's Dollo Ado camps: arid, with less land for farming, a different refugee population (Somali) and tighter rules on refugees' work and movement than Uganda's settlements, but the same Village Enterprise program and grants. The carry is 0.85, a little deeper than the 0.92 core_evidence_adj makes for the core trial carried to new settings, because the population and setting differ more; 0.81 in all, 0.57 to 0.95.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, core program (Kenya, Uganda, Rwanda) (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: Internal validity, about 0.95: two independent, pre-registered randomized trials of this program itself (and a third, IPA's in Uganda, with the same consumption effect), large samples, disbursement verified; consumption is self-reported, and the impact-bond trial's outcome paid the charity, which may have raised delivery quality during the trial. External validity, about 0.92: the FY2025 core program is wider than the trial (northern Kenya's drylands, Rwanda's government-linked delivery, digital delivery pilots), against which the trial ran partly during COVID-19 lockdowns (which lowered its Ugandan effects). 0.87, 0.7 to 1. Anchor: the site's GiveDirectly model takes recipients' consumption gains from its trials at face value (1) and cuts the weaker spillover evidence to 0.6 × 0.8; this program's trials are as strong as GiveDirectly's for recipients but measure a smaller effect, of a program that has since changed more.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS Uganda (internal validity)
rows.explainer: DREAMS Uganda is the trial's own program in the trial's own settlements (later cohorts than those studied), so only the internal-validity part of core_evidence_adj (0.95): self-reported consumption, a household-level design in which some controls joined savings groups.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment, DREAMS Tanzania (internal and external validity)
rows.explainer: The DREAMS trial's all-household effect carried to Tanzania, where local community-based organisations deliver DREAMS after Village Enterprise trains them, for naturalised former refugees and their neighbours: a new setting and delivery channel, so the same cut as core_evidence_adj (0.95 × 0.92), 0.7 to 1.

rows.label: Yearly fade of the consumption gain
rows.explainer: The program's own evidence shows no detectable fade over 0.5 to 2.5 years: across the core trial's seven cohorts there are no significant differences in consumption effects except the COVID-hit Cohort 4 (report printed p. 20, PDF p. 22). Inside that, Kenya's later cohorts (surveyed sooner after the program) had larger effects than earlier ones, a hint of fade, and Uganda's the reverse (the report finds the evidence for its lockdown explanation of Uganda's pattern mixed, printed p. 21, PDF p. 23); in DREAMS the cohort followed longest had the largest effect. Anchors outside the program: consumption gains about as large in year 3 as in year 2 in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015) and growing to year 7 in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al. 2017), against Uganda's cash grants for trades, whose earnings gains were gone between year 4 and year 9 (Blattman, Fiala and Martinez 2020), a fast fade after year 4. 5% a year as the best guess: no fade seen so far, some later as the light package's businesses face competition; 0 to 20%. The trial's cohort comparison can't tell 5% from 10% a year; the choice rests on the outside anchors, most of which show gains holding for several years.

rows.label: Years the consumption gain lasts, counted from the program year
rows.explainer: How long the (fading) gain lasts before it stops. The core trial measured households 6 months to 2.5 years after the program (3.5 years after it started) and still found gains; DREAMS only to 18 months. Anchors: Raising the Village, a similar livelihoods program in Uganda, is counted 3 years (1 to 6) on the site, GiveWell's best guess from a trial with one year of follow-up; heavier graduation programs kept their consumption gains at least a year after implementation ended in six countries (Banerjee et al. 2015), 7 years in Bangladesh (Bandiera et al. 2017) and 10 years in India (Banerjee, Duflo and Sharma 2021); cash grants to start trades in Uganda raised earnings at 4 years but the controls caught up by year 9 (Blattman, Fiala and Martinez 2020). This program has more follow-up than Raising the Village's trial but a lighter package than BRAC's, so 8 years with the fade above (worth about 6 years of the full gain), 3 (what the trial saw) to 12.

rows.label: Total ln(consumption) gain per person, present value
rows.formula: ((households_kenya * core_kenya_ln_gain_year + core_uganda_households * core_uganda_ln_gain_year + households_rwanda * core_rwanda_ln_gain_year) * core_evidence_adj + dreams_uganda_households * dreams_ln_gain_year * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj + households_tanzania * dreams_ln_gain_year * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj + households_ethiopia * dreams_ethiopia_ln_gain_year * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj) / households * pv_annuity_due(1, (1 + $discount_rate) / (1 - fade_rate) - 1, persistence_years)
rows.explainer: Each group's yearly gain (Kenya, Uganda and Rwanda from the core trial, DREAMS Uganda and Tanzania from the DREAMS trial, Ethiopia from its refugee subgroup), times its branch's evidence adjustment, weighted by its households, over the years it lasts, fading each year and discounted at the shared rate (the first year in full). A recurring income gain, as the template's explainer describes, not a one-off transfer: the seed grant is invested in the business, and the trials measure consumption from its returns.

rows.label: Spillover benefits to non-participants, as a share of participants' benefits
rows.explainer: Neither trial measured effects on non-participating neighbours: the impact-bond trial compared whole villages (so spillovers inside treated villages are invisible), and the DREAMS trial randomized households inside the same communities, where controls joined some savings groups and borrowed from participants (2% of control households joined a savings group, and some borrowed from participants: DREAMS report, PDF pp. 42-44), which if anything biases its effect down. Cash entering a village raises local incomes (Egger et al. 2022 for GiveDirectly's far larger transfers); Village Enterprise's transfers are a tenth of that size per household. 10% as the best guess, 0 to 40%. Business competition with non-participants is a negative share in unmodelled_benefits_adj.

rows.label: Mortality benefits as a share of consumption benefits
rows.explainer: Neither trial measured deaths, so 0, as the template asks for programs without mortality evidence; the high end allows for a child-mortality effect of a 6-18% consumption rise, much smaller than the effect GiveWell credits GiveDirectly's US$1,000 transfers with.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (internal and external validity), outcome-weighted average of the branches, for reading only
rows.formula: ((households_kenya * core_kenya_ln_gain_year + core_uganda_households * core_uganda_ln_gain_year + households_rwanda * core_rwanda_ln_gain_year) * core_evidence_adj + dreams_uganda_households * dreams_ln_gain_year * dreams_uganda_evidence_adj + households_tanzania * dreams_ln_gain_year * dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj + households_ethiopia * dreams_ethiopia_ln_gain_year * dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj) / (households_kenya * core_kenya_ln_gain_year + core_uganda_households * core_uganda_ln_gain_year + households_rwanda * core_rwanda_ln_gain_year + (dreams_uganda_households + households_tanzania) * dreams_ln_gain_year + households_ethiopia * dreams_ethiopia_ln_gain_year)
rows.explainer: The outcome-weighted average of the branch evidence adjustments (core_evidence_adj, dreams_uganda_evidence_adj, dreams_tanzania_evidence_adj, dreams_ethiopia_evidence_adj), for reading only: each branch's own row is applied in ln_gain_per_person (Convention 4). After all adjustments the model credits about this × 0.95 × 0.98 of the trials' effects on participants, before shared credit and the wait.

rows.label: Share of the outcome that wouldn't have happened anyway
rows.explainer: The trials' effects are already net of their control groups, who got what they would have got anyway (food rations in the settlements, government transfers in Kenya). Below 1 only for government graduation programs (Kenya's KSEIP II, Rwanda's national graduation strategy) now expanding into the same areas, which may reach some households Village Enterprise enrols.

rows.label: This charity's share of the resources behind the outcome
rows.explainer: Village Enterprise pays for the training, grants and mentoring itself, and its subaward to Mercy Corps is in its cost. Outside its cost: Mercy Corps' own funding for DREAMS' market-systems work, the government staff who help target and deliver in Rwanda and Kenya, BOMA's lead role in Kuza Jamii, the unpaid time of savings-group leaders, and in Tanzania the community-based organisations that deliver DREAMS after Village Enterprise trains them. Together judged at about 15% of all resources (0 to 30%).

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Share of reported households who get the program as studied
rows.explainer: The FY2025 count is Village Enterprise's own. In the impact-bond trial, 95.7% of households offered the program received at least the first grant, verified by IDinsight; 98% received the first grant in DREAMS. The effects used are on participants (treatment on the treated), so non-take-up is already out of them; this covers only counting error in the charity's own figure and the FY2025 households in programs cut short by the 2025 US stop-work order (Nawiri in northern Kenya and the USAID-funded Rwanda program, about 12% of program spending, some of whose households may have missed the second grant or mentoring; the annual report doesn't say how many). 0.98, 0.88 to 1.

rows.label: Leverage and funging
rows.explainer: Village Enterprise is funded by many private donors and foundations, and the loss of USAID funding in 2025 left gaps it had to fill (annual report p. 3), so little of a gift displaces other money; outcome funders and governments co-funding the model pull some in. 1, 0.85 to 1.1; the governments' wider adoption is in unmodelled_benefits_adj, not here.

rows.label: Years from a donation to the first consumption gains
rows.explainer: Spending happens through the year (about half a year on average), and each cohort's four months of targeting and training come before its first grant (audited statements, note 1); gains start after the grant. Village Enterprise holds about a year of spending in cash and investments, but its net assets grew by only $0.5M in FY2025, so a gift is spent rather than added to reserves. 0.75 years, 0.4 to 1.25.

rows.label: Discount for the wait until the gains start
rows.explainer: The wait discounted at the shared rate.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above; the evidence adjustments are applied per branch in ln_gain_per_person.

rows.label: Benefits and harms not modelled, as a share of modelled value
rows.explainer: Each effect not modelled, with its sign: assets left when the consumption gain ends (net assets +US$40 per household in the core trial, +US$184 in DREAMS) +5%; governments adopting the model beyond the households Village Enterprise trains (Kenya's KSEIP II with US$127M from the World Bank, Rwanda's national strategy, three Kenyan counties; spending on this technical work is in the cost) +5% (0 to 30%); nutrition gains for malnourished children in the Nawiri program (6% of spending) beyond consumption +2%; women's empowerment and wellbeing beyond consumption are not added (valued through income); business competition with non-participating traders -2% (to -10%); wastage, fraud and diversion of grants -2% (GiveDirectly's model takes the same -2%). Net +13%, -7% to +45%.
